tier_reason: Peer-reviewed papers (SageAttention, ICLR 2025; SageAttention2, ICML 2025) report kernel throughput wins over FlashAttention2; the venue is stated in the README and corroborated by search results listing the ICLR 2025 poster page and the arXiv PDF headed 'Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2025', though the papers themselves were blocked here. The repo has a public harness (bench/README.md, bench_qk_int8_pv_fp8_cuda*.py) and names each GPU, but the CUDA/nvcc version and flags used for the plots are not stated, so not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README news item (2025-02-15): 'On RTX5090, SageAttention reaches 560T, 2.7x faster than FlashAttention2!'; (2025-01-28) on Hopper (H100, H800, H20) it 'matches the speed of FlashAttention3-FP8' with better accuracy. README end-to-end table, CogVideoX1.5-5B on an NVIDIA H20: FlashAttention2 25'34'', FlashAttention3 17'32'', FlashAttention3-FP8 12'14'', SageAttention 12'07'' (about 2.1x over FlashAttention2 and 1.45x over FlashAttention3, derived from page data). GitHub description: 'speedup of 2-5x compared to FlashAttention'. Per-GPU kernel TOPS plots are images only. ICLR 2025 abstract (seen via a search result; arXiv blocked here): OPS about 2.1x FlashAttention2 and 2.7x xformers; SageAttention2 abstract (same source): about 3x FlashAttention2 and 4.5x xformers on RTX 4090.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 4,000 stars, 521 forks (GitHub page); PyPI sageattention latest 1.0.6 (2024-11-20)
corrections.caveats: Kernel TOPS plots exclude the quantization and smoothing time (README note), so kernel-only ratios overstate the end-to-end gain; end-to-end is shown only for selected video/image/language models. The 2.7x figure is for one GPU (RTX 5090) against FlashAttention2 only; on Hopper it only matches FlashAttention3-FP8. Speedup comes from INT8/FP8/FP4 quantization, so it is a lossy approximation of FP16 attention (the authors report negligible end-to-end metric loss). The code is Python/Triton/CUDA behind a PyTorch API, not a C++ library. The README tells users to 'pip install sageattention==2.2.0', but PyPI lists only releases up to 1.0.6; the PyPI wheel carries a BSD-3-Clause license string while the repository LICENSE is Apache-2.0. CUDA version and nvcc flags used for the published plots are not stated.

notes: README numbers match the record. The arXiv, OpenReview and iclr.cc pages are blocked by egress here, so peer review rests on the README plus search-result listings (as with earlier wave-8 B entries). Last commit 2026-01-17 confirmed (active). Baseline FlashAttention is itself a wave-8 entry (dao-ailab/flash-attention).

tier_reason: Vendor-run DLPerf benchmark (Oneflow-Inc) with public scripts per framework and a report that names the host CPU (Xeon Gold 5118), V100 GPUs, CUDA 10.2 and driver, but no compiler or build flags for any framework, so it falls short of A; first-party, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: DLPerf README summary (4 nodes x 8 V100-SXM2-16GB; report published Oct 2020). ResNet-50 v1.5 FP32 bsz=128: OneFlow 12411.97 img/s vs NGC MXNet 11233.92, NGC PyTorch 10917.09, PyTorch 10021.29, NGC TensorFlow 1.x 9514.64, TensorFlow 2.x 9418.44 (about 1.14x vs NGC PyTorch and 1.10x vs NGC MXNet, derived from page data). AMP bsz=256: OneFlow 33141.02 vs NGC MXNet 30713.68, NGC TensorFlow 1.x with XLA 29171.69 (bsz=224), NGC PyTorch 22551.16 (about 1.47x vs NGC PyTorch and 1.08x vs NGC MXNet, derived). BERT-base AMP bsz=max: OneFlow 15724.70 (bsz=160) vs NGC TensorFlow 1.x with XLA 11650.0 (bsz=96) and NGC PyTorch 10349.12 (bsz=96), about 1.35x and 1.52x (derived); without gradient clipping OneFlow 17210.63 vs MXNet 14822.31 (about 1.16x, derived).
corrections.hardware: 4 nodes x 8 Tesla V100-SXM2-16GB; Intel Xeon Gold 5118 @ 2.30GHz, 384 GB RAM, InfiniBand 100 Gb/s EDR (Mellanox MT27700) per node; Ubuntu 16.04.4, CUDA 10.2, driver 440.33.01 (DLPerf report v1)
corrections.baseline: NVIDIA NGC 20.03 containers (MXNet 1.6.0, TensorFlow 1.15.2, PyTorch 1.5.0a0) running NVIDIA DeepLearningExamples, plus stock PyTorch 1.6.0, TensorFlow 2.3.0, MXNet 1.6.0 (gluon-cv/gluon-nlp), PaddlePaddle 1.8.3 and MindSpore official model scripts
corrections.caveats: Benchmark run and published by the OneFlow vendor (Oneflow-Inc/DLPerf) in Oct 2020 with OneFlow 0.2.0 against 2020-era framework versions; none has been re-run on current releases. Compiler and build flags are not stated for any framework. OneFlow's margin over the strongest baseline (NGC MXNet) is small: about 1.10x FP32 and 1.08x AMP on ResNet-50. Baseline caveats: TensorFlow 1.x AMP used bsz=224 (OOM at 256), PyTorch (non-NGC) AMP is missing, MXNet BERT lacks gradient clipping. The README summary lists NGC MXNet FP32 at 11233.92 img/s while the report's 4x32 row gives 11331.93, an internal inconsistency. Last commit 2025-08-20, so stale.

notes: README numbers match the record; the v1 report adds host CPU, CUDA and container versions. Corrected hardware and baseline versions; status stays stale (last commit 2025-08-20, about 13 months ago).

tier_reason: First-party benchmark by the RTNeural author with public code (RTNeural-compare src/benchmark.cpp, run_bench.sh, raw logs in results/bench_{stl,eigen,xsimd}.txt) and a named CPU (Intel Core i7-8700B), built as CMake Release, but the compiler and its version are not stated, so not A. The arXiv paper 2106.03037 appears to be a preprint only (no venue seen), so not B.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Exact values from RTNeural-compare results/bench_*.txt (real-time factor at 48 kHz, one sample per call, higher is better). LSTM size 4: RTNeural Eigen static 268.3x real time vs ONNX Runtime 1.42x and libtorch 0.375x (about 189x vs ONNX Runtime, derived from page data); size 64: Eigen static 6.46x vs ONNX Runtime 1.13x and libtorch 0.262x (about 5.7x, derived). GRU size 4: xsimd static 338.2x vs ONNX Runtime 1.46x and libtorch 0.370x; size 64: Eigen static 8.67x vs 1.23x and 0.273x. Dense size 4: xsimd static 6164x (STL static 5969x) vs TensorFlow Lite 151.5x, ONNX Runtime 7.51x, libtorch 2.33x (about 41x vs TensorFlow Lite, derived); size 64: Eigen static 76.8x (xsimd static 67.9x) vs TensorFlow Lite 40.7x (about 1.9x, derived), ONNX Runtime 6.84x, libtorch 1.75x. The STL backend at size 64 reaches only 1.01x (LSTM) and 1.37x (GRU) against ONNX Runtime's 1.13x and 1.23x, and 8.69x vs TensorFlow Lite's 40.7x on Dense, so it is slower there.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: CMake Release build (run_bench.sh: -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release), C++17; compiler and version not stated. Baselines: prebuilt onnxruntime-osx-x86_64 1.15.1 and tensorflowlite_c 2.14.0; libtorch version not stated.
corrections.caveats: Benchmark by the RTNeural author on one x86 Mac (i7-8700B), one sample per call, so per-call framework overhead dominates the libtorch, ONNX Runtime and TensorFlow Lite figures; the advantage shrinks as layer size grows, and the STL backend falls below ONNX Runtime (LSTM size 64) and well below TensorFlow Lite (Dense size 64). Baselines were timed only in the STL-backend run; the Eigen and xsimd runs were RTNEURAL_ONLY builds, so those ratios compare separate runs. Compiler not stated, libtorch version not stated. The reference paper (arXiv:2106.03037) is a preprint.

notes: Replaced plot readings with exact values from the raw result logs; the record's approximations were right except Dense size 64, where the about-75x figure belongs to the Eigen backend (xsimd static is 67.9x). Metadata confirmed: BSD-3-Clause, 848 stars, last commit 2026-08-20 (active).
